text:
A baseline takes three months to approve and about three months to stop being used. After 18 years I think we build most of them for the wrong audience.

The baseline is written to pass review: logic checks, DCMA, float, the client's planning specification. It passes. Then site starts working from a three-week lookahead in Excel, and the P6 file is updated once a month for the report.

Two plans. The one we report and the one we build.

You can usually tell within a few months:
• out-of-sequence progress grows with every update
• actual dates arrive in one batch, the day before the report
• supervisors have never opened the level 3
• each recovery schedule keeps the same end date with shorter durations

What has worked for me:
1. Build the baseline with the people who will execute it. Supervisors in the room, not only planners.
2. Keep the logic at the level site makes decisions: area, system, test pack. Not tens of thousands of activities nobody reads.
3. One plan. The lookahead comes out of the schedule, not typed beside it.
4. Track out-of-sequence progress every month as a health check of the plan itself.

A baseline is not a deliverable. It is the agreement on how we will build. If site does not recognise it, it is not an agreement.

Be honest: on your project, does the three-week lookahead come out of P6 or out of Excel?

#ProjectControls #PrimaveraP6 #Planning #Scheduling #EPC

images.alt: Card: Two plans, the one we report and the one we build. Reported: P6 baseline, thousands of activities, updated monthly, opened by planners. Built: Excel lookahead, three weeks, updated daily, opened by site. Make it one plan: the lookahead comes out of the schedule.
